title: The unions of Abba and Ima: Shabbos, Yom Tov and the week of the mind, up to the birth of souls
overview:
The last chapter showed three ways *chachma* and *bina* receive from the *Keser*: from the *mazalos*, where a person loves a thing for itself and so sees every detail; from the *zro'os*, where the intellect is the emotions' puppet; and from *Nehi*, where it is a tool for a goal it cannot question. This chapter shows the same range in *Abba* and *Ima* themselves.

Their inner union is *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, leisure for the mind. On *Shabbos* *chachma* rests and sees G-dliness as it is, before it is named; on *Yom Tov* *bina* enjoys the inner point, through symbols and *mitzvos*. Their outer side, the *middos* of the intellect, is the mind that leans to a verdict: felt without reasons in *Yisroel Saba*, like Rav who kept silent, and explained in *Tevuna*; and its *Nehi* weighs how to carry the verdict out, with conviction or without. The inner union is like a couple who simply enjoy each other; in the *Shema* it is reached by *mesirus nefesh*. Souls are born only from a union that reaches the *mazalos*, as only a great sage who knows an idea at its source can teach it to a child.

sections.title: The light goes down through Abba and Ima themselves: from the mazalos to the outer Nehi
sections.summary: Chapter 25 explained the ways *chachma* and *bina* receive from the *Keser*: from the *mazalos*, from the *zro'os*, or from *Nehi*. This chapter shows the whole range of *Abba* and *Ima* themselves, from their inner intellect that receives from *Arich* to their outer *Nehi* that goes into *Zeir Anpin*; and the level they receive from decides how true the intellect is.

blocks.text: Now that the last chapter explained the different ways that *Chabad* (*chachma*, *bina* and *daas*) can receive from the *Keser* (crown): either from the *mazalos* (lit. the flows; he compares them to hairs), or from the *zro'os* (the arms), the *middos* (emotional attributes) of the *Keser*. If it gets from the *mazalos*, it is getting from the *Chabad* of the *Keser* and even higher, all the way to the essence of the *Keser*. Or it can get from the *middos* of the *Keser*, the *vav* (the six emotions) that are enclothed in the *zro'os* of *Arich Anpin*. Or it can get in the normal way, from the *Nehi* (*netzach*, *hod* and *yesod*) of *Arich Anpin*, since, as was said, the *Nehi* of the higher goes into the lower.

blocks.text: In this chapter we are going to explain three different levels of the *yichud* (union) of *Abba* and *Ima*: *chachma* and *bina* not as faculties but as *partzufim* (statures), when they come together to work together to understand an idea. They are called *trein rei'in d'lo misparshin*, two companions that never part: they are always working together. As soon as you get an idea in *chachma*, right away you start to analyze it, order it, categorize it and name things in *bina*. And whenever you try to analyze something in *bina*, you always try to find the generalities and similarities in *chachma*, to see how it all fits together. You are always using both together. But when they come together to produce ideas, they can come together on three general levels, and that is what this chapter discusses.

blocks.text: "It seems to me," Rabbi Walters says, that these three levels of the union correspond to the three levels that the last chapter said *chachma* and *bina* receive from: whichever level it receives from, that is the level of its union. The middle one, the *zro'os*, is like a puppet: when a person's intellect is blinded by emotion, or by political things. Above that is when it gets from the *mazalos*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: A quick review of the last chapter. If a person's desire, when it comes to intellect, is for the intellect itself, it comes from the *Chabad* of the *ratzon* (will): he wants the *Chabad*, so the *Chabad* is true, and he is pursuing the true idea. If it comes from the emotions, the intellect is being used as a puppet, to prove the emotions, to justify them. If it comes from *Nehi*, it is being used as a tool. That is normal, like a *merkava* (a chariot, a vehicle for the will): it is objective, but it is only allowed to figure out a means to an end, how to accomplish the goal the *ratzon* wants. It cannot challenge the goal; that is not up for discussion. That is normal everyday intellect. When you go to your job, your intellect is not usually thinking, "Should I be doing this? Is this the right job for me?" You just think how to do your job: that is the *Nehi*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: On *Shabbos* you are supposed to be on the level of the *mazalos*. When the intellect gets from the *mazalos*, the inner *taanug* (delight) is hidden in there too, and it makes a person very smart. The *mazalos* are of the *Chabad* of *Arich Anpin*, of the *mocha stima'a* (the hidden brain) and the hidden *bina*, but their root is really in the liquid of the brain, and really in the skull, which is higher than the liquid. So, as was said about how *Atik* is enclothed in *Arich*, it is really coming all the way from *Atik*, from the *middos* of *Atik*. That is what it says, *pnimiyus Abba* (the inner side of *Abba*) is *pnimiyus Atik*: when the intellect comes from the *mazalos*, it is really coming from the *middos* of *Atik* that are enclothed in the *gulgalta* (the skull), the liquid and the membrane.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: That is why a person with a big talent for something is one whose intellect receives from the *mazalos* in this thing. It means that he loves the thing itself; he sees it as an end in itself. So when his intellect looks into it, it enjoys every detail and looks at every detail, because he is learning about it and thinking about it for the sake of the thing itself, not as a means to an end. The more something becomes just a means to an end, the less you care about it, and the more you just look at it in a superficial, general way. So you pass over the details that would make you really good at it, really smart at it.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: That is why somebody like the Rebbe, even naturally, would be very smart at everything. And this is also true about us: when you learn *Chassidus* and really take to heart what it is saying, it will make you very smart in everything. Why? Because what makes you stupid at things is that you do not really pay attention to the details; you just look over it generally, like a *girsa* (rote) thing.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.title: The kid with the hockey cards
blocks.text:
When you go through life you see most things as not very important, and you do not really think about them or care about them. It is like the kids in school who are not so smart. But when it comes to something they really enjoy... His teacher told him about a kid he knew who was not so good at math, not so good in school in general, but he had these hockey cards, and he knew every statistic for every player. He could add up all the things and figure out all the different percentages; he knew how to figure all that stuff out, because he loved it.

So if a person only enjoys the football, everything else in life he just goes through on autopilot, doing the bare minimum to get by. He is not going to notice the details, he is not going to be interested, and he is not going to really understand it.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: But *Chassidus* teaches you to find the G-dliness in everything, which is the idea of *iyun* (close analysis). When the first chapter talks about *iyun* and *girsa*, the real thing it is talking about is how you go through life in the world: whether you stop and try to find the word of G-d, the *Elokus* (G-dliness), in things, or whether you just pass over it. When you see that everything has *Elokus* in it, you see things as an end in themselves, as having essential value, and so you are interested in the thing itself. You care about all its little details, you spend time on it, and that makes you able to be very good at everything; especially when you see how they connect.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: That is the idea of the *mazalos* pointing to it: your essential *taanug* goes into the thing, then the senses, and that means that you actually want the thing itself. And that is also why the *mazalos* are like hairs. The *tzimtzum* (contraction) of a hair means that the whole essence comes over, just in a tiny drop. So when you look at something as a little example of the essence, you see everything as just an example of G-dliness. You feel that it is *mamash* (actually) G-dliness: it is not a means to an end, it is the end in itself, just in a little way. It is a *metzumtzam* (contracted) thing of the end, but it is actually something of the real goal. And that makes a much, much bigger intellect, and a bigger *taanug* in it.
blocks.outOfPlace: Tape 30 reads no line of the chapter: it is his introduction to the whole chapter, placed under its first line.

blocks.text: If it is only the *zro'os*, the *middos* going into *chachma* and *bina*, that is like somebody who is very smart and is always looking and thinking into the things he sees in the world, but he is looking with an agenda. He is always looking to use everything to prove something, to prove his view.

blocks.title: Proving the Rebbe is Moshiach
blocks.text:
Say somebody is always trying to prove that the Rebbe is *Moshiach*. That is the way he learns a *sicha* (talk), but really the way he does everything: if he is good at it, he will try it with everything. He is not appreciating the thing itself as having merit or value, or a lesson. He really sees the thing as something outside of his point, but he is using it.

There are two ways to use it: the way of the puppet, or just as a means to an end. A means to an end is that since he wants to spread that the Rebbe is *Moshiach*, he will learn about publishing and radio and whatever, so he can use them to publicize it. But he really does not care about them at all.

There is a means to an end that is not connected to the thing, and a means to an end that is connected to the thing. Say he is just trying to translate something about the Rebbe being *Moshiach* into a different language, and he is trying to figure out the best word. There he is using his mind as a means to an end where it does not really matter: it is not something that could affect the essential thing. The level of the *middos* means that he is worried that something could affect the essential thing.

blocks.title: Parents who overlook what their child did
blocks.text: So he feels threatened, and he has to twist it. Say parents love their child. When they see their child doing something wrong, a lot of times their intellect will twist the thing and try to overlook what the child did wrong. A person does the same thing with himself: because he loves himself, he sees himself as being a certain way, and if he sees that something he did contradicts the way he wants to be, he tries to cover it up. It is already a given in his mind that he is good, or that his child is good, and since this thing threatens that, he feels he has to wrestle with it. That is the level of the *middos*: he does not see this thing as the essential thing but as a symptom of it.

blocks.title: Driving to work
blocks.text:
So it is necessary for it to be in line with the essential thing, and threatening if it is not. Whereas the *Nehi* is something that is not threatening. Say you are figuring out how to drive to work. You are using your intellect, but if you have to take a detour and go a different way, that does not threaten your essential beliefs and values; you do not really care. You just want to get there so you can get the money.

Whereas the intellect that made you decide that you have to go to work is a bias of love toward your family: you feel you have to provide for them. The intellect of how to get there is already cold. The intellect of "I love them, so I have to provide for them" is hot. It is not your actual love for them; you could really still love them even if you do not go to work. But it is like a sign: if you really love them and you do not want to provide for them, that does not look great.

blocks.text: That was the last chapter. Now: **now we have to understand the way the light goes down further, how it goes through the ten sefiros of Abba and Ima themselves**. The *mashal* (analogy) of *Abba* and *Ima* is a father and a mother.

It is true that this applies any time the *Keser* goes into *chachma* and *bina*. Nevertheless it is discussed *davka* (specifically) here, in *Atzilus*, because when we talk about the *partzufim*, the five or six of them however you count them (*Atik*, *Arich*, *Abba*, *Ima*, *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva*), we are usually speaking about *Atzilus*. Why? Because higher than *Atzilus* is before the *Tikun* (the world of Repair), and the main *Tikun* is in *Atzilus*. Before the *Tikun* there is not yet the division of the lights into vessels, ten into ten and so on, so there is no *partzuf* yet; there are just the points of *Tohu* and the like. The *Adam* of *Adam Kadmon* is kind of like a *partzuf*, but not a particular one: it is a general *partzuf* for everything. So the main *partzufim* are in *Atzilus*.

And why is it not in *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*? Because the way the *partzufim* come out into those worlds is not the real *partzuf*. It is only the revelation of it in something separate, because those worlds are already like thought, speech and action, which are separate from the essence.

blocks.title: The student in class and at recess
blocks.text: What is a *partzuf*? It is a person's ten powers being used for a certain thing. When a person is using all ten powers to learn, that is like *Abba*: he has a learning personality. You could see somebody in the classroom and see his learning personality, then see him out at recess, just socializing, and it could be a totally different thing. When he is doing his hobbies and his passions, what he enjoys, that is like an *Atik*-*Arich* *partzuf*. Then there is just dealing with him day to day, whether he is a nice guy, what you normally mean when you say a person's personality: that is his *Zeir Anpin*. And how good he is at speaking and doing things, whether he is a charismatic speaker: that is like a *Nukva*. Those *partzufim* are mainly the way the person's conscious mind is revealed in his body, the soul in the body in a conscious state.

That is *Atzilus*: the consciousness the way it is revealed in the body. Higher than *Atzilus* is the subconscious. Lower than *Atzilus* is when it comes outside of you into expression, when you say something or do something: there is an expression of the *partzufim* there, but it is not alive anymore. So the *partzufim* are mainly in *Atzilus*. There are of course discussions of *partzufim* higher and lower than *Atzilus*, but plain *partzufim* are in *Atzilus*, the world of *Tikun*, the world of the *partzufim*; and that is why they are discussed here. In chapter seven too, when he lays out the beginning of the *hishtalshelus* (the chain of descent), that is where he puts the *partzufim*. So this does apply anywhere, just a little differently.

It would not be the proper place to explain it earlier or later, because there it is not the main thing stressed at that level. Now we have to understand how the light goes down. What does "the light" mean? The revelation of the person's self: how his self-expression comes down and remains transparent through the ten *sefiros* of *Abba*, the intellect.

blocks.text: **From the level of the pnimiyus of the intellect of chachma and bina**: the inner side of the *mochin* (lit. brains, the intellect) is when they receive from **chesed and gevura of Arich Anpin**. And all the more so **when they receive from the mazalos of Arich Anpin**, which is even more inner. But that is rare; it is not even normal intellect. What is normal intellect? The emotions, and then the *Nehi*. Most people barely even tap into the *mazalos*.

Most people, even when they do philosophy, are only on the level of the *middos*. That is why most people, when they philosophize, are not really trying to pursue the truth so much as emotionally defending and substantiating their world view. That is why they get emotional about it when they discuss it: they feel threatened that the conclusions might affect the way they live their life, or the way they view themselves as being good. They are trying to prove their natural bias and inclination. The very fact that they approach it trying to come to a conclusion one way or the other already shows that they are on the level of the *middos*, as opposed to the essential thing.

*Chassidus* is not really telling you good or bad about anything. It is just telling you what it is: trying to understand very clearly what it is and how everything fits together. That is why it lets you find the good in everything, but in a detached way. Most people do not really have this. The real question is when to use which one; not which one is true, but when to use which one.

But there are also people who really have a *chush* (a sense) for something, people who are really geniuses at things. That is a whole other type of person: passionately into something, he really loves it, and he enjoys all the little details, like a real artist. That is a *mazalos* guy: he sees the thing as an end in itself and loves it, with its details. If a person is going to be like that with philosophy, he has to just love truth, love understanding the way things are; not even so much to come to conclusions about anything, but as a pure thing that is an end in itself, a *lishma* thing, like pure science. And even if he brings it to application, he will not see that as something separate: he will be interested in seeing how it is when it is applied. He is still not doing it as a means to an end.
The real *mazalos* thing is *Chassidus*. That is what *Chassidus* is. All the other levels of Torah, even, are not really like the *mazalos*; that is why they are all *halacha* (law) and such things.

blocks.text: So: for sure when it goes to the *mazalos*, and **all the way down to when only the external Nehi of Abba and Ima**, which are enclothed in the *mochin* of *Zeir Anpin*, give, as it is in *Etz Chaim*. All the way from the inner *mochin* of *Abba* and *Ima*, which receive from the *Keser*, up to the *mazalos* of the *Keser*, and then all the way down to the outer side of *Abba* and *Ima* that goes into *Zeir Anpin*. You want to see how *Abba* and *Ima* go all the way up and how they go all the way down: "the whole spectrum of *Abba* and *Ima*'s *Abba*-and-*Ima*-ness." That is this chapter. The last chapter talked about the different ways the *Keser* can give to *Abba* and *Ima*; now we explain the different levels of *Abba* and *Ima* themselves, what it looks like when they go all the way up to receive from the *mazalos*, and when they go all the way down to give into *Zeir Anpin*.

sections.title: Shabbos and Yom Tov: the inner union of chachma and bina, for its own sake
sections.summary: The inner *mochin* of *Abba* and *Ima* are like *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, leisure for the mind. *Shabbos* is called *kodesh* and *oneg*: *chachma* resting, seeing G-dliness as it is, as an end in itself; *Yom Tov* is only *mikra kodesh* and *simcha*: *bina* enjoying the inner point of the idea, through symbols and *mitzvos*. Where the two meet, *havein b'chachma v'chacham b'vina*, is the inner union of *Abba* and *Ima*.

blocks.text: **And the inyan is known, that it's like Shabbos and Yom Tov.** *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* are a *mashal* for the inner intellect of *Abba*. Why? **Because Shabbos is called holy**, *kodesh*, and *chachma milsa b'garmei*: **chachma is a thing onto its own**. What does that mean? That it is an end in itself. *Kodesh* means that it is removed from all other things, that it does not need anything else: the pleasure is in it itself, it is enjoyable, it is fun, and so it is an end in itself, not a means to an end. That is why *Shabbos* is *kodesh b'oneg*, holy in delight: *chachma* is a thing on its own.

*Shabbos* is when you rest your *chachma*. What does it mean to rest? What is the difference between work and leisure? It is not so much what you are doing; it is whether you want to be doing what you are doing, whether you enjoy it, whether it is an end in itself. You have pleasure in it, so you would do it even if you did not get the money. Work means that you do not like what you are doing, you would rather not do it, but you need money, so you have to.

That is *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* in general: they are leisure. Only that *Shabbos* is the leisure, the resting, of *chachma*, and *Yom Tov* is the resting of *bina*, because there are different types of leisure. On *Shabbos* you have fun with *chachma*; on *Yom Tov* your *bina* has fun. *Shabbos* is the inner side of *chachma*, which is an end in itself. You can also use your *chachma* to figure out what is right and what is wrong and how to act: that is the outer side of *chachma*, for the week.

On *Shabbos* you give your *chachma*, your creative ability, a break from figuring out ways to make money, and even from figuring out *halachos*. It gets to do what it likes to do, and what your *chachma* likes to do is to see G-dliness in things in a pure way: pure science, not applied science. It is work for your *chachma* to have to figure out applications and deal with things that are not a subject it enjoys.

During the week the mentality is that things are bad, and you have to be *mevarer* them (sort them out), figure out what is good and what is bad and stay away. *B'chachma isbariru*: with your *chachma* you are able to sort out the right way to do things. But that means you are seeing everything as not really G-dliness. The real thing you want to be doing is sitting and learning *Chassidus* in yeshiva, but you have to go out and learn law, or do business, things you do not like to do, or even eat and sleep. So it sees most of the days as a drag. On *Shabbos* it is a whole different *hisbonenus* (contemplation).

On *Shabbos* you look for the actual G-dliness in everything, in the way of *b'chol derachecha da'eihu* (know Him in all your ways). You see everything as having an essential G-dliness to it, and you do not have to do anything to it to fix it up. It essentially has it, because G-d made it, so it has a certain G-dly wisdom in it, and you just look for that wisdom. That is why on *Shabbos* you are able to actually use the taste of things. During the week you use food only for its energy, but on *Shabbos* you actually enjoy the taste, because you look at G-d's wisdom, how He chose to make it taste; that too is a revelation of G-d's wisdom. And first of all, it is a *mitzva* (commandment) to do it on *Shabbos*: you are not allowed to do it during the week, and on *Shabbos* you definitely are supposed to. That is the *mitzva*.

blocks.title: Playing the game and watching the video
blocks.text:
During the week the *mitzva* is to be *mevarer* the world. Imagine you are playing a basketball game. While you are playing, you are not supposed to say, "Oh, it doesn't really matter, it's just a game." No: you are supposed to care, put in your best and try hard, and not break the rules and give the other guy a free shot because he messed up. That ruins the game. But when the game is over and you are relaxing afterwards, watching the video, then you should just enjoy even your mess-ups, enjoy the whole thing, and not be all competitive and a sore sport.

G-d has both things. The six days of the week you are supposed to be playing the game. On *Shabbos* you are supposed to stop and rest and just enjoy the beauty, like taking a vacation. You are supposed to be thinking about Torah, and even your *hisbonenus* is supposed to be not like during the week, when you are trying to sort out your *middos*, but just to appreciate that everything is *Elokus*. It is a different story.

phrases.he: והוא בחינת פנימית אור אבא
phrases.en: This is the *pnimiyus* of the *or Abba*,

phrases.he: (שהוא פנימית עתיק יומין,
phrases.en: so that's the *pnimiyus* of *Atik Yomin*.

phrases.he: וזה שנאמר
phrases.en: this is what it says:

phrases.he: וקראת לשבת עונג,
phrases.en: you should call *Shabbos* pleasure, or that you should bring pleasure into *Shabbos*,

phrases.he: וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר בענין ג' סעודות דשבת באריכות)
phrases.en: as explained elsewhere at length about the three *seudos* of *Shabbos*,

blocks.text: **This is the pnimiyus of the or Abba**, the inner side of the light of *chachma*. First of all, it is the inner desire in *chachma*, this pleasure: you are thinking about something you really enjoy; in this case, G-dliness. Also, the real revelation of the person, mainly in *chachma*, is when he uses his *chachma* in something he really loves; that is where the main light of it is. He is not saying that the person becomes the *chachma*, but that this is the inner side of the light of *chachma*: when he really enjoys it. That is when it receives from the *mazalos*. It shows what he really enjoys, his inner side; whereas the outer *chachma* just shows the *chachma*, not what he likes. You do not see what he is choosing.

That is like the difference between the *mitzvos* and the world. The world is like the outer *chachma*: you see G-d's wisdom, how He chose to make it, but you do not see what He chose to represent Himself, what He chose to connect Himself to. That is the *mitzvos*.

The inner side of *Abba* is the inner side of *Atik*: **so that's the pnimiyus of Atik Yomin**, the inner pleasure. **This is what it says:** *v'karasa laShabbos oneg*, **you should call Shabbos pleasure, or that you should bring pleasure into Shabbos**, because the *taanug* is revealed in the *chachma*. **As explained elsewhere at length about the three seudos** (meals) **of Shabbos**: how they are the inner *taanug*. Why three? There is one for *Chakal Tapuchin Kadishin* (the field of holy apples), one for *Atik Yomin*, and one for *Zeir Anpin*. "It's the idea of, I guess, the revelation of the *taanug* coming into all of those things. I don't know much how it's connected."

phrases.he: ויום טוב נקרא מקרא קדש,
phrases.en: and *Yom Tov* is called not *kodesh*, it's only called *mikra kodesh*.

phrases.he: בחינת שמחה,
phrases.en: which is *simcha*,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב אם הבנים שמחה
phrases.en: like it says, the mother of the children rejoices,

blocks.text: **And Yom Tov is called not kodesh, it's only called mikra kodesh** (a calling of holiness). That means it is only a spreading forth of it, as opposed to the thing itself: a lower level. On *Shabbos* everything, the *chachma*, goes up. On *Yom Tov* only the *bina* goes up, so the *chachma* is still working. That is why on *Yom Tov* you are allowed to do *borer* (sorting) for *ochel nefesh* (preparing food), and on *Shabbos* you are not.

*Yom Tov* is like analyzing the world to understand it: you are not just seeing the G-dliness in its purest state, you are trying to understand it in human intellect. You are already bringing the idea down to relate to the world, so you have to take things from the world to compare it to, make *meshalim* (analogies), order it, see how it appears in different examples. That is the idea of *ochel nefesh*: you have to make food to get the sustenance from. You have to take things from the world to feed the G-dliness: *meshalim* and the things of human intellect. So you see the G-dliness, but indirectly; it has already come down from its essential state, and that is *bina*.

There is also a *chumra* (stringency) that *Yom Tov* has over *Shabbos*: *nolad* (a thing newly come into being) is *muktza* (set aside, not to be handled) on *Yom Tov* and not on *Shabbos*. Because *Yom Tov* is the thing of analyzing: you want to take what you already have and analyze it, not deal with new information, with *chiddushim* (new insights). That is work for *bina*. So *nolad* is *muktza*. On *Shabbos* it is *chachma*, and coming up with new things is part of the essence of *chachma*, so *nolad* is not *muktza*.

You see that *Yom Tov* is a lot more fun than *Shabbos*, but not as restful. You can carry your *sefarim* around, you can make food; it is easier to party on *Yom Tov* than on *Shabbos*. But *Shabbos* has a certain thing: you do not worry about anything, because you cannot do anything. You do not have to worry about making food. The way it is, that is the way it is, and you just enjoy it the way it is.

*Yom Tov* is called *mikra kodesh*, **which is simcha** (joy). *Oneg* (delight) is the revelation of *kodesh* directly: *Shabbos* is a revelation of the *oneg* directly, so it is called *oneg*; and *Yom Tov* is its spreading forth, which is called *simcha*, when it comes into your *yeshus* (sense of self). As was explained in chapter four, *chachma* makes *bittul* (self-nullification) and *bina* makes *simcha*. *Chachma* makes you lose yourself: you have the pleasure, but the pleasure is from the thing, so you lose your *metzius* (existence) and feel its existence; you are not feeling yourself, you are feeling the thing. *Simcha* is when you understand it in your own vessels, so you feel that you have it, that you are on top, you are the boss. You have something very big, so you have a big *simcha*.

That is *mikra kodesh*, **like it says, the mother of the children rejoices**, because that is the idea of *bina*: associating something with something outside of itself. That is *mikra*, calling: you are giving it a name, connecting it. You are making a connection to the essence, but it is really an artificial thing that you are doing. You are not even applying it to the week yet; applying it would already be the week. You are making it represented by something, finding ways to represent it, so it is not the thing itself anymore but represents the thing itself. That is human intellect: you make symbols and names and systems and order to represent the idea, but it is not the thing itself anymore. So it is called *mikra'ei kodesh*: you call it *kodesh*, but it is not essentially *kodesh* itself.

That is why on *Yom Tov* there are *mitzvos* that you have to do, while on *Shabbos* there are no *mitzvos* you have to do: you just sit there and do nothing. On *Yom Tov* we want to express our connection to G-dliness; on *Shabbos* the point is that it is essential, and you do not have to do anything to show it. It is just there. You do not even have to make *kiddush*: "the *mitzva d'oraisa* is not to say *kiddush*, it's to enjoy things, to have wine and stuff like that. I don't think that the *mitzva* though is to say the *kiddush*." The *mitzva* is that you should appreciate that G-d made the world and rested on *Shabbos*, that everything has that level of G-dliness in it, and you should recognize it; so you say it verbally, to make yourself conscious of it in a practical way, to be *mekadesh* the day. It is true there are a few things you are supposed to do: good food, nice clothes, set everything nicely. But there are no real *mitzvos* of the day.

sensitivity.reason: States as halacha that the Torah mitzva of kiddush is not verbal but enjoyment and wine ("I don't think that the mitzva though is to say the kiddush"), against the usual ruling; a reader might act on it.

The point of the day is that you should appreciate that G-d made the world and rested on *Shabbos*, that everything has that level of G-dliness in it, and you should recognize it; and so you say it verbally, in *kiddush*, to make yourself conscious of it in a practical way, to be *mekadesh* the day. It is true there are a few things you are supposed to do: good food, nice clothes, set everything nicely. But there are no real *mitzvos* of the day.

blocks.text: It is not like you have to make a *sukka* and have a *lulav* and *esrog*, or eat *matza* and have a whole *Seder*. On *Shabbos* you are just supposed to eat what you like, what you enjoy. For example, on *Shabbos*, if you do not enjoy wine, you are not supposed to have wine. On *Yom Tov* you have to have wine whether you enjoy it or not, because you cannot have *simcha* without wine. Once you make it that it has to come through a certain way, you have already said: this is the way we are going to represent this thing. So it is already a little out of your hands.

sensitivity.reason: Says as a rule that on Shabbos one who does not enjoy wine is not supposed to have wine, which a reader might take as a ruling on kiddush wine.
sensitivity.publishable: It is not like you have to make a *sukka* and have a *lulav* and *esrog*, or eat *matza* and have a whole *Seder*. On *Shabbos* you are just supposed to eat what you like, what you enjoy. On *Yom Tov* you have to have wine whether you enjoy it or not, because you cannot have *simcha* without wine. Once you make it that it has to come through a certain way, you have already said: this is the way we are going to represent this thing. So it is already a little out of your hands.

blocks.text: *Chachma* is like, "Just be yourself, man. We accept you as you are." And the same with the world: the whole point of *Shabbos* is to get you to stop trying to change things, and just enjoy and appreciate the way things are. Enjoy the world as it is. G-d made the world perfect; you do not have to do anything, just enjoy it. No rules. The only rule is not to spoil the fun: you have to play along with the enjoyment. Do not ruin the vacation by thinking about work. "That's the only rule here: you have to have fun."

On *Yom Tov* you have already decided that we are having fun by playing a certain game, and you have to play by the rules. *Yom Tov* already shows our connection to G-d through the *mitzvos* of *matza* and *sukka*. But all those *mitzvos* are special, general *mitzvos* that show our essential connection to G-d and our essential *emuna* (faith). *Matza* shows the *emuna*, which is why it is flat and without taste; it represents the *chachma*. The same with the *sukka*: it shows that even though we do Torah and *mitzvos*, we recognize that they are not an end in themselves. They are a temporary thing, like the *sukka*, and we see through it: we really just want to connect to G-d and do what He wants, and we do this to express that. The point of the *Yamim Tovim* is to reconnect and recognize that the things we do during the week, the *mitzvos*, are like the intermediate between the *chachma*, the *Shabbos*, and the week: to see how they are an expression of the *chachma*. That is the *bina* thing.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת מוחין דאימא שמקבל מאבא,
phrases.en: which this is the *mochin* of *Ima*, the intellect of *bina*, which receives from *chachma*.

phrases.he: כי השביתה דשבת הוא בחכמה גם כן
phrases.en: the resting of *Shabbos* is in *chachma*,

phrases.he: דהיינו בפנימית אבא, בחינת כח מה אין דחכמה
phrases.en: which that is the inner part of *chachma*, the *koach MaH*, which is the *ayin* of *chachma*,

phrases.he: קודם שמתפשט ליש בהשגה דבינה
phrases.en: even before it comes into be understood in *bina*.

blocks.text: *Em habanim semeicha*, **which this is the mochin of Ima, the intellect of bina, which receives from chachma**. For **the resting of Shabbos is in chachma** as well, *chachma*'s own resting: in the inner side of *Abba*, the *koach MaH* (the power of "what"), which is **the inner part of chachma, the koach MaH, which is the ayin of chachma**, its *ayin* (nothing), **even before it comes into be understood in bina**. That means that on *Shabbos* the *koach MaH* of *chachma* is revealed: you are just perceiving things in their essential state, before you can explain them, just taking them in as they are, before you interpret, organize and name.

blocks.title: Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain
blocks.text:
Have you ever read the book *Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain*? "It's a very good book." It teaches you how to draw, and it is a very good book about *chachma* and *bina*, if you want to learn about them. The whole point of the book is to teach you how to go into the *chachma* mode of thinking, and that is the secret of drawing. The secret of drawing a thing exactly the way it is, is to train yourself to look at it and think about it exactly the way it is, instead of making names for its parts and drawing the parts you named.

When a person looks at a face, he sees eyes, nose, ears, mouth, hair, glasses, neck, forehead, and he draws a symbol for each of those parts. So it does not look like the actual person; it looks like symbols for a person. When you draw what you are actually seeing, depending on the angle it could be all distorted and look nothing like the symbol you have for it. So you draw what you see. You have to train yourself to draw what you see and not to name it: just lines and shadows, lights and darks and colors, instead of eyes and nose. The problem is also that most of the details have no names, so when you name things you do not draw those details, and that is also why it does not look right.

When you look at it in an abstract way, as it is, without naming and categorizing it, it stays whole. By naming it you are automatically picking what you consider important and what you do not, which is why *Atik* is revealed in *bina*: what you care about is revealed by the distinctions you make, which affects how you think of things, name them and talk about them. It is like the blot test: the *chachma* is really an uninterpreted blob, seen as it is, and the interpretation you give it is really coming from you, not from the thing, because you could interpret it differently, cut it up differently, name it differently. What you consider important is what you will look for and find. So it is really a way of looking into the person: it shows you what is important to him, what he is always interested in. That is how *bina* reveals the *Atik*, what he really enjoys.

phrases.he: וכן בינה בבחינת פנימית,
phrases.en: and the same thing that on *Yom Tov*, which is the *pnimiyus* of *bina*,

phrases.he: הוא עומק נקודת המושג כו',
phrases.en: that's the *omek nekudas hamusag* of *bina*.

phrases.he: כידוע שיש אין חכמה בבינה ובינה בחכמה
phrases.en: that there is the *ayin* of *chachma* goes into *bina*, and the inner thing of *bina* is in *chachma*.

blocks.text: **And the same thing that on Yom Tov, which is the pnimiyus of bina**: **that's the omek nekudas hamusag** (the depth of the point of the concept) **of bina**. On *Yom Tov* you focus on the depth of the concept, as opposed to the proofs, the examples or the applications; just on the inner point of the idea. That is the resting of *bina*: *bina* enjoys the inner point. In the same way, on *Yom Tov* we focus on the inner point of the *mitzvos* and of the sorting out of the world: what is the real point of it, the goal.

blocks.title: The object of the game
blocks.text: What is the goal of the game, the object of the game? In *bina*, the object of the game is to win by getting the most points. In *chachma* it is just to have fun, and you do not really care; you can have fun even if you do not win. When you come to *bina*, you now associate that it is fun to win, or something like that: it already comes into a certain form of what is fun. *Chachma* can have fun doing anything. So even though on *Yom Tov* you do not do a lot of work, because it is not practice time (practice is when you do all the work), you still have to do some work, because you have to win the game. You still have to do things in a certain way.

For it is known **that there is the ayin of chachma goes into bina, and the inner thing of bina is in chachma**. When you go to the inner point of *chachma* and *bina*, they connect: the *chachma* goes into the *bina* and the *bina* into the *chachma*. Whenever you analyze or understand something, you are analyzing and understanding the thing itself, so there is always a *chachma* in there. And even when you get the *chachma*, there is always some noticing of details and a certain amount of interpretation, because you have to perceive differences to see how it differs from other things. So there is always some *bina* in it. You cannot really have one without the other; it always goes both ways.

phrases.he: והיינו הבן בחכמה וחכם בבינה,
phrases.en: that in the *chachma* itself, you'll be able to find the ability to make the distinctions and then explain it, and from the explanations, you'll be able to get the inner point, which is the *chachma*.

phrases.he: שזהו בחינת יחוד פנימית דאבא ואמא
phrases.en: That's the inner *yichud* of *Abba* and *Ima*, *chachma* and *bina*,

blocks.text: That is what *havein b'chachma v'chacham b'vina* (understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding) means: **that in the chachma itself, you'll be able to find the ability to make the distinctions and then explain it, and from the explanations, you'll be able to get the inner point, which is the chachma**. **That's the inner yichud of Abba and Ima, chachma and bina**, when they come together for the inner idea, to get its inner point. When *chachma* and *bina* work together just to understand the inner truth of an idea, that is from the *mazalos*: when it comes from the *mazalos*, it makes an inner union of *Abba* and *Ima*.

blocks.title: Three levels of a marriage
blocks.text: By the way, the *mashal* for this whole thing, as it says, the simple one, is a father and a mother. When people are married, there are three general levels on which they relate to each other. There is just spending time together, because they enjoy spending time together; it is not for any other purpose, the relationship itself is an end in itself. That is like the inner union of *Abba* and *Ima*: both the mental connection and the enjoyment they have in each other. The man has to do things to come down to the *bina* and recognize the *bina*, and the woman has to recognize the *chachma*. You have to try to express your love in little, tangible, symbolic things, like flowers and little notes; that is already an expression. But it is for yourselves. It is not like raising kids, where you have to work together, a practical relationship; or doing your taxes together, taking out the garbage or washing the dishes. Those are practical things that you have to do.

blocks.title: Stuck in traffic, and raising kids
blocks.text:
You could do those in a way of *pnimiyus* too: if you appreciate that it is an opportunity to build a relationship and spend time together. When you are stuck in traffic somewhere, you appreciate it: "Oh, it's an opportunity, we get to spend time. Who cares?" You could have that attitude all the time, just enjoying each other's company and doing things together. But from *Nehi* up to the inner side, it is a means; it goes all the way from the bottom to the top. *Nehi* mode is, "Man, I got to get there quick."

In between is raising kids. The main thing about a father or a mother is that they are the father and mother of kids. There is a level where they connect to each other that is higher than the kids: that is the inner side. The regular thing, in the middle, is that the purpose of marriage is to make a family, have children and raise them. And then there is going to work and doing the taxes, the practical things they have to do just to live together. That is not the real purpose; it is a means to an end, to keep the house going, with money and food and everything set up.

sections.title: The outer flow: the middos of chachma and bina, intellect that leans
sections.summary: When *chachma* and *bina* flow outward into their *Chagas* and *Nehi*, the intellect is a means to an end. The *middos* of *chachma*, its *vav ketzavos*, are the mind applied to a case or leaning toward kindness or judgment; they shine into the *middos* of *bina*, which give them good reasons, before they are born as emotions of their own.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן בחיצונית השפע דחכמה ובינה בחג''ת נה''י כו',
phrases.en: On the other hand, when the *chitzoniyus hashpaa* is going into *Chagas* and *Nehi*

phrases.he: כמו מדות שבחכמה
phrases.en: Like the *middos* of *chachma*

phrases.he: שנקרא בחינת ו׳ קצוות דאבא
phrases.en: which are called the six directions, the six dimensions of *Abba*

blocks.text: **On the other hand, when the chitzoniyus hashpaa** (the outer flow) **is going into Chagas** (*chesed*, *gevura* and *tiferes*) **and Nehi**, it is not an end in itself but a means to an end. **Like the middos of chachma, which are called the six directions, the six dimensions of Abba**, the *vav ketzavos*: the way *chachma* is expressed within time and space, in a particular form. It is not the thing itself any more but its expression; it is circumstantial.

blocks.title: The law and the case
blocks.text: Say you are learning a *halacha* about something as an abstract law. Then you have an actual case, and that case is within certain circumstances of time and space: that is like the *vav*. When you apply the abstract law to this case, that is *chachma* going into the six directions of *chachma*: how the law is applied in this case. And when you have a precedent, you do the opposite: you extrapolate the *chachma* from the example, from the particular case.

phrases.he: כמו חסד שבחכמה,
phrases.en: Like *chesed sheb'chachma*,

phrases.he: דהיינו כח שכל המטה כלפי חסד
phrases.en: like that you can use the intellect to lean towards *chesed*,

phrases.he: או כח שכל אחר שמטה כלפי דין כו'
phrases.en: or you have another *koach* of the *sechel* to go towards *din*.

blocks.text: And *middos*: **like chesed sheb'chachma** (kindness within wisdom), meaning **that you can use the intellect to lean towards chesed, or you have another koach** (power) **of the sechel** (intellect) **to go towards din** (judgment). So you can use your intellect to prove emotions. But that is not the real thing of intellect. The real thing of intellect is just to understand how things are. When you use it to prove your views, to use the facts to prove your views, you are using it for your own benefit.

phrases.he: ומאירים בחסד וגבורה דבינה
phrases.en: And the *chachma* shines into the *bina*, so the *middos* of *chachma* shine into the *middos* of the *bina*,

phrases.he: דהוא בא בהשגה בטוב טעם בהסבר לזכות ולחוב
phrases.en: So, in *bina*, it becomes very well explained, good reasoning for whether for merit or for guilt.

phrases.he: ונקרא מדות שבשכל המושג,
phrases.en: These are called the *middos*, the emotions of the intellect, which is understood,

phrases.he: קודם שנולדו במהות בפני עצמן (כמו שיתבאר)
phrases.en: before the *middos* become actual their own thing, before they become just *middos* without intellect, which is *Zeir Anpin*, like we'll explain later

blocks.text: **And the chachma shines into the bina, so the middos of chachma shine into the middos of the bina**, which then come up with explanations to make it sound rational. There is a certain point a person has that substantiates the *midda* and supports it, why he thinks it is good or why he thinks it is bad. Sometimes a person has a certain point why he feels it is good or bad, but he is not so good at explaining it, because he does not have such a good *bina*. That does not mean it is not true; some people are just better at arguing, at formulating their thoughts logically.

**So, in bina, it becomes very well explained, good reasoning for whether for merit or for guilt.** **These are called the middos, the emotions of the intellect, which is understood, before the middos become actual their own thing**, before they become just *middos* without the intellect, which is *Zeir Anpin*, as will be explained later about *Zeir Anpin*: how they are born.

sections.title: Shatik Rav: silence is a fence for wisdom
sections.summary: When a person sees that a thing is so and cannot explain it, that is the *middos* of *chachma* before they shine into *bina*, like Rav who kept silent. Silence protects a *chachma* from being argued away, and it keeps the mind open to the source of all ideas, so that being quiet "gets you double".

blocks.text: We spoke about *nolad* on *Yom Tov*: that is the *Gemara* in *Beitza*, about an egg laid on *Yom Tov*, and that is the *Gemara* where it says *shatik Rav*. He could not explain the difference: that the one does not disprove the other, that there is some distinction between those two *halachos* so that you cannot extrapolate one from the other. But he could not find it, he could not explain it. So he was quiet. He did not retract his ruling, but he did not argue further, and some other sage came and explained it. That is the *mashal* for *Yisroel Saba* (lit. Israel the elder), for the *middos* of *chachma*: this thing, *shatik Rav*.

blocks.text: *Ushtika seyag l'chachma*: why is a person quiet when he has a *midda* of *chachma* and cannot explain it? It is a fence that protects the *chachma*. The simplest meaning, there in *Pirkei Avos*, is that if you keep your mouth shut you will learn a lot: if you sit and listen and observe, you learn a lot, and once you start opening your mouth you stop yourself from learning. That is the plain meaning. But it does not fit so well with the words: why is that called **a fence for the wisdom**? It does not seem like the right analogy. A fence implies that you have something and want to protect it, while this is telling you that you will not get it if you keep opening your mouth. So here he explains it further: when you have a *chachma* and you keep your mouth shut and do not give a reason for it, that protects it. Once you give a reason for it, it is open to be argued with and disproven.

blocks.title: The Rebbe's advice for a debate on TV
blocks.text:
This is what the Rebbe told, he thinks, Rabbi Hollander, when he was asked to discuss or debate Judaism with a Reform rabbi on TV or something like that. He asked the Rebbe what he should do, because he did not want to give the Reform rabbi any credence, to make it look like he believed in Reform at all or considered him a legitimate rabbi. The Rebbe told him that the first thing, as soon as he gets up there, he should say: "I do not agree with your stance at all, and I do not recognize you as a rabbi. Now, let's discuss the issues."

In other words, he starts off with the premise: no matter what happens here today, you should know that it is not open for debate; it is axiomatic that you are not a legitimate rabbi and that I do not agree with your whole religion, and it is not Judaism. You are Jewish because you were born Jewish, but this whole ideology has nothing to do with Judaism. If you want me to try to prove it to you, I can try, but even if I fail at that, that is not up for debate. That is one example of how silence is a fence for wisdom.

blocks.text: The other thing is that when you are trying to get an idea, you are quiet, because when you look into the *chachma* you are just seeing the thing itself, and trying to interpret it will disturb that. You have to just let it in as it is. That is also why a person who gets a flash of an idea is quiet.

*Mishtuka b'trei* (silence is worth two). "Maybe you have a name for this in Latin": a principle in *halacha* that sometimes a person makes a claim and gets $100, but if he had kept quiet and not claimed anything he would have got $200, because his claim in some way impairs his rights. He ruined it for himself by claiming what he claimed. By opening his mouth he got one; if he had been quiet he would have got two. **Being quiet gets you double.**

What does that mean here? That the *bittul*, the silence, in a way gives you a better understanding. *Chassidus*, for example, is really not interpreting anything; it is just understanding as it is. That is also the difference between G-dly intellect and human intellect. So in a way it is being quiet, not telling you its interpretation, and that really gives you double: you understand it better. Because with **this bittul of the koach MaH of chachma, where you just experience it as it is, without interpreting it**, you get it objectively, and so **you're able to go to the source of all the intellect**, which is called the hidden *chachma*, **and you can get out a new idea**, because you did not limit it to a certain box. You are free to take it out in any way. Once you attach it to a reason or an explanation, you limit it: if that reason gets disproven, it looks bad for the whole thing. Or it makes it hard for you to make a *chiddush*, because you only understand it within a certain context or example, and it is hard for you to take it out of that.

sections.title: Netzach and hod of Abba: the scales of the mind and the strength of conviction
sections.summary: The *Nehi* of *Abba* is the scales of the intellect, the *kelayos yo'atzos* that weigh how a verdict should be carried out. *Netzach* and *hod* are the mind's legs: a person who is *takif b'daito* stands by his view, and one who is not falls easily from guilt to innocence. Only from the *Nehi* of *Abba* in the *Nehi* of *Ima* come the *mochin* of *Zeir Anpin*.

phrases.he: ובחינת נה''י דאבא, היינו בחינת מאזני השכל והחכמה, איך שיבא הדבר חכמה לידי השפעה בבחינת כליות יועצות כו'

blocks.text: *Nehi* of *Abba* is the scales of the intellect and the wisdom, how the thing of *chachma* will come to be given over. Once you have figured out with the intellect whether a thing is good or bad, you have to figure out how to actually apply it. It is like the difference between the verdict and the sentence. *Chachma*, *bina*, *chesed* and *gevura* are like a verdict: was it good, or is it bad? But that is still kind of abstract. Then you have to figure out how we can act upon it: what are we going to do about it, how can we bring it out? That is the scales of the intellect, which weigh out how the thing should come out.

And this is the idea of the *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice. When it comes to actually doing something, should you do it with gusto, gung-ho, or should you be scared and timid, with restraint? *Netzach* would want you to give the full thing, the maximum prescription, whatever it is, good or bad: the full extent of the law. *Hod* would want you to hold back a little, because you consider that it would be better, or maybe because you are scared it will be too much.

blocks.title: The lashes and the first offender
blocks.text:
Say you are evaluating how many lashes to give the man. *Netzach* wants to give him all of them, but *hod* is scared that you will kill him. So you have to weigh it out, because the whole purpose is not to kill him; the purpose is that he should live and be better. So you have to be careful not to give too much and ruin his opportunity.

The same thing in court. A lot of times with a first offender, especially a young offender, they do not want to throw him in jail, because they want him to be reformed and have a normal life, not rot away in jail; that is not productive. So they try to be lenient the first time. But if he keeps doing it, they throw the book at him. Those are the kidneys that give advice.

blocks.text: This is the strength in the mind that is called *takif b'daito* (firm in his mind): **the force of your views, when you are strong-minded, when you're strong in your opinions**. **Like the legs, they have the strength to hold up the whole body, so too netzach and hod of the chachma hold up the actual intellect.** **And the opposite**: when **a person is not strong-minded, he can easily fall from his reasoning from guilt to innocence**, from **impure to pure**; **and the same thing with the netzach and hod of Ima**.

In other words, if you do not have a strong *netzach* and *hod*, even though it is just the outer side of the intellect, you will not have the guts to seal it one way, because you can always argue the other side.

This is like liberalism, or pluralism, that kind of thing: they do not have strength in their view, they do not have enough conviction to stand up for what they believe in and take a stance (that is the *mashal* of the legs, "following all these English correspondences") and say, "That's it, this is it, and you are wrong, and therefore we..."

blocks.text: And to have a legal system, by the way, this is very important: you have to feel strongly enough that this is right and that is wrong to take responsibility to punish somebody for it. You have to have strength in your opinion, and that comes mainly from *netzach* and *hod*. In theory there is truth to the different sides, but when it comes to actually doing it, first of all one way is the best way to do it; and even besides that, if you want to actually do it, it is more important to do it one way, even if it is not the best way, than to keep finding different possible ways to do it.

So if you are a proactive, task-oriented person, that is the thing. Sometimes, when you have a system, it does not matter so much whether it is the best system. It is better to have a system and a leader that you listen to and follow, and get things done, than to sit around thinking up which is the best system. It is true that in theory you could always find a better way and improve it, but you are never going to get anything done like that. That is why *Elul* is a time when you are supposed to stop and make a *cheshbon hanefesh* (an accounting of the soul), but the rest of the year you are supposed to focus mainly on doing, and not keep second-guessing yourself that maybe you should be doing something else. You cannot do that all the time.

blocks.text: In general, only from the *Nehi* of *Abba* enclothed in the *Nehi* of *Ima* is the source of the *mochin* of *Zeir Anpin*, the *middos* that are below the intellect. Once you have a *midda*, there is a certain intellect of how and when you should have that *midda*. When you are just going through day-to-day life, you are not thinking about the meaning of life and your life goals all the time. You already figured that out at some point, figured out your priorities, and based on that what you should like and what you should hate. Now you just have that as an *uvchein* (a conclusion), and your whole intellect is just how to react to whatever goes on around you.

blocks.title: The job and the family
blocks.text:
A person has the *ahava rabba* (great love) in the *Chagas* of his will: he loves his family, and that goes into his intellect and makes him want to get a job to support them. But once he is on the job, the *Nehi* of the will goes into the *Nehi* of the intellect: he has to figure out how to do his job well, and he cannot be thinking about his family the whole time; he has to think about his job. That practical intellect comes out as the *mochin* for the *middos*: he will be happy about making a profit and scared to lose money. He has a certain intellect of just how the *middos* should be.

That comes from the *Nehi*, but from the *Nehi* of *Abba* as it goes into the *Nehi* of *Ima*. He has a certain feeling of how he should do things based on his intellect, a kind of gut feeling: that is the *Nehi* of *chachma*. Then it has to go into the *Nehi* of *Ima*, where he can understand it a little and see how to apply it, so that he can explain to himself when to have the *midda* and when not to, and based on that he is able to have the *middos*. This will be discussed later, with the *middos* of *Zeir Anpin* and how they are born from the intellect.

sections.title: Two unions: for their own sake and for new mochin; Shabbos, the Shema and mesirus nefesh
sections.summary: *Abba* and *Ima* unite either in their inner side, for themselves, like a couple who simply enjoy each other, or in *Nehi* alone, to give new *mochin* to *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva*, like workers calling a manager. That is the difference between *Shabbos* and the week. In the *Shema*, *Havaya Elokeinu* is the inner union and *Havaya Echad* the union below it; it is reached by *mesirus nefesh*, as the ten martyrs raised *MaN* to the inner side of *Abba*.

phrases.he: וידוע פרטי עניני יחודים דאבא ואמא
phrases.en: Now we're going to explain the *pratei yichudim* of *Abba* and *Ima*,

blocks.text: **Now we're going to explain the pratei yichudim** (the particular unions) **of Abba and Ima.** It was explained that in *Abba* and *Ima* there are the *Chabad*, the *Chagas* and the *Nehi*, the three main levels. The *Chabad* of *chachma* and *bina* is like *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*. The *Chagas* is like the inner thing of the week, and the *Nehi* is like the regular thing of the week. The last two are like the difference between the verdict and the sentence: one figures out whether this is good or bad, and the other what you should do about it.

phrases.he: בין כשהוא בבחינת הפנימית לצורך עצמן,

phrases.en: before it goes into the *middos*,

phrases.he: ובין כשמתייחדים לצורך מוחין חדשים לזעיר אנפין ונוקבה,

blocks.text: **Whether it's a yichud in the pnimiyus for themselves**, which is like *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, **which is the gimmel rishonos** (the first three), **the Chabad or the Keser, chachma, bina of the mochin, before it goes into the middos**: a union in the theoretical essence of the idea, where *chachma* and *bina* come together just to understand the idea, not for an application yet. The *mashal* is a father and a mother, who are also husband and wife: they have a certain relationship that precedes their being a father and a mother. It is just for themselves, spending time together and talking and going out to eat. There is a reason, just not a reason outside of the relationship; it is just for the relationship, for themselves, not for the *middos* yet.

blocks.title: Calling the manager
blocks.text: Or **whether getting together to make new mochin for the middos**, for *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva*, to figure out what to do. They say, "You know what? We got to call a manager here, we got a problem." The *middos* get instructions and just run on autopilot based on them, but sometimes they need new information, because they run into a problem. Then the *middos* need to be fixed up, so you need to get new *mochin*: you have to call a manager who actually has brains. The regular workers do not have brains; they just follow policy. If you want to do something that requires brains, you have to go to the brain people, and they have to figure out what to do. That union, to bring out new *mochin* for *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva*, how the emotions should be and how thought, speech and action should be, how to act *b'poel mamash* (in actual practice), **which is just the Nehi**, is the outer side of the union.

phrases.he: וזהו ההפרש בין שבת לחול כו'
phrases.en: this is the difference between *Shabbos* and *chol*.

blocks.text: **This is the difference between Shabbos and chol** (the weekday). On *Shabbos* you focus on just the essential connection of *chachma* and *bina*. Your learning on *Shabbos* is supposed to be just to know G-d, not to figure out how to act: like learning Torah *lishma* (for its own sake). Learning Torah *lishma* is not learning *halacha l'maaseh* (law for practice); that is not what is called learning Torah *lishma*. The *mitzva* of knowing the *halachos* so that you know how to act is a separate *mitzva* from learning Torah. There is a *mitzva* to learn Torah just to know G-d's wisdom, as an end in itself.

And the same with your *hisbonenus* in *davenen* (prayer): it is not supposed to be an attempt to change your *middos*, to make you have a love so that you change your *middos*. It is supposed to be just appreciating G-dliness, for its own sake: *avoda* of the mind, not for *birur* (refinement), not even to refine your mind, just *lada'as Havaya levad*, just to know G-d. That is *Shabbos*. During the week the main focus is on refining your *middos*: learning *halacha l'maaseh*, and contemplating *Chassidus* in order to come out to a practical thing in *avoda*. Those are the two types of union in the way your mind comes together: you can learn a theoretical thing for itself, or learn it to apply it to something else.

שמשם יהו״ה אחד,

blocks.text: In *Krias Shema*, the intention in *Havaya Elokeinu* is in the inner side of *Abba*. When we say *Shema Yisroel Havaya Elokeinu*, *Havaya* is *chachma* and *Elokeinu* is *bina*: it is the union of *Abba* and *Ima*, their inner side. Your *kavana* (intention) is to contemplate how everything in the world is a revelation of G-d, and that this is an end in itself: G-d is our G-d, so everything has a G-dly essence, and you do not have to do anything to it. We are essentially connected to G-d and do not have to do anything to connect to Him; we are just trying to reveal that connection, but we have it essentially. *Elokeinu*, our G-d: He is essentially our G-d. *Havaya*, higher than any limitations, decided that He is going to be *Elokeinu* in the way of *Havaya*, higher than reason and intellect. Normally *Elokim* means nature and limitations, but the point is a union of *Havaya* and *Elokeinu*: G-d, as He is higher than all limitations, chose that our nature should be connected to Him.

Just *Elokeinu* would mean that we would have to work to get it. *Chachma* means the thing as it is from the side of the essence, and *bina* means the way it is associated with something, as in a language. So *Havaya* is the revelation of G-d, and *Elokeinu* means that He made it our nature to reveal Him, to be a vessel for that. But that we are a vessel for it, we do not have to work for or deserve; that too comes in the way of *Havaya*. "The Jew's connection to G-d is unconditional." It is above reason and unconditional; that is *Havaya Elokeinu*. The nature of a Jew is that he is G-dly, and that's it. That is just fact. It does not depend on anything, and it is not a means to something: it itself has value. That is a complete statement.

That is what he explains: in *Shema Yisroel Havaya Elokeinu* you should realize that *Havaya*, which is higher than nature, is our G-d. And when you see how G-d is in you (that is the whole thing: when you learn about the *hishtalshelus* you really only see it in you, not in the world; you see it the way he explains how it is in you), when you realize that G-d is really in you and you are able to find that in you, then it tells you *Havaya Echad*: G-d is in everything else in the same way. Once you see how it is in yourself, you are able to see how it is in everything else by extension. Once you see the *nimshal* (what an analogy stands for) in you, once you know how the *hishtalshelus* works in you, you know how it works in everything, so you really know everything. As the Arizal says, somebody who knows how to make *yichudim* can know whatever he wants to know, because once you know how to see it in you, you see that it is really the same thing everywhere else.

So *Havaya Elokeinu* is the inner side of *Abba*: not for a reason, not applying it, just appreciating the reality that you are connected to G-d, as an end in itself, without trying to do anything about it. **As a result of that, Havaya Echad, which is the idea of the yichud of Zeir Anpin and Nukva.** *Havaya Echad* is the union of *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva*: you should realize how G-d is one with the world, that He controls everything, which is the *middos* coming into *Malchus*, *hashgacha pratis* (Divine providence over every detail). But to realize that, you first have to realize that the world is being created by G-d and so essentially reveals Him, because there is nothing else except for G-d, so everything is by His choice and reveals Him. That makes a big change in your *middos* too, and in the way you look at how the world is run. If you realize that every moment is being recreated by G-d's choice, then you realize that everything is *hashgacha pratis*, that everything has a lesson, and that nothing can stop you from doing what G-d wants. All these realizations come out of it, about the way the world is and the way your *middos* should be.

blocks.text: That new *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva* comes **when they get this new mochin**. The reason your *middos* are the way they are now, and the reason that the world seems limited to a certain thing (you think that to make money you have to do it this way), is that you have messed-up *mochin*: you think that *teva* (nature) is a set thing. But once you realize the reality, that G-d is recreating the world every moment and it is all just coming from Him, then automatically your emotions become such that you are not scared of anything except G-d, and you are not *nispa'el* (overawed); you see the world differently. **So they can give birth.**

phrases.he: והיינו במסירת נפש דקריאת שמע,
phrases.en: And this is accomplished in the *mesirus nefesh* of *Krias Shema*.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן בתורה ומצות בלא מסירת נפש
phrases.en: when a person does Torah and *mitzvos* without *mesirus nefesh*,

phrases.he: אין היחוד רק בחיצוניות דאבא ואמא בזעיר אנפין ונוקבה, כמו שכתוב במקום אחר

blocks.text: **And this is accomplished in the mesirus nefesh** (self-sacrifice) **of Krias Shema.** When a person has *mesirus nefesh*, he reveals his essential connection to G-d that is not based on anything, not for any particular of Torah and *mitzvos*. Then he is able to apply that to make a change in the way his *middos* are going to be.

That is the whole idea of *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur*, and then *Sukkos*. The *teshuva* (return) of *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur* is to reveal this *mesirus nefesh*: that you have a connection to G-d that is higher than the Torah and *mitzvos*, that "you don't care about the Torah and *mitzvos*, you just care about G-d", and that this essential connection has to be higher than Torah and *mitzvos*. Once you realize that, you are able to do Torah and *mitzvos* with *mesirus nefesh*: you do them because you have this essential connection, which is the whole reality of you and of the world, and the whole purpose is just to reveal it. So you know that nothing can stop you from revealing it and nothing can separate you, so you are not scared and not overawed by anything, and then you are able to do Torah and *mitzvos* properly.

blocks.title: A child cannot yet have children
blocks.text: You have to get a new worldview, a new perspective. The main problem is that before, you were trapped by a false worldview, and that gave you the inhibition that limited your *middos* and your deeds, made you a *baal middos*. It is like a *mashal* of a child who cannot have children until he gets *tosefes mochin* (added intellect): until he matures intellectually, enough to have the *daas* to have children. Until he gets that, he cannot. In order to give to somebody outside of him, he has to be able to feel his essence and be conscious of it, and not be worried that he is going to lose it.

That is the *mesirus nefesh* of *Krias Shema*; whereas **when a person does Torah and mitzvos without mesirus nefesh**, he does not reveal G-d's essence. When a person first has the *mesirus nefesh* and then does Torah and *mitzvos*, he reveals G-d's essence. Without it, in a way he is not really doing a *mitzva*: he is doing just the external action of it, and it is not coming from the inner side of the *mochin*, from who he is and the real truth, from being dedicated to some higher thing. It is just that that is the way he was trained; he still believes what he originally believed and is still committed to serving himself the same way he always was. He thinks his best chance of getting lollipops is to listen to his mommy and *tatty* and do Torah and *mitzvos*. In a way it is *mitzvas anashim melumada* (a commandment of men, learned by rote): still within his nature, and not really for G-d.

So it does not really change him; it is still within his limitations. And the reciprocal effect from G-d's side is that G-d does not do miracles for him, does not change nature for him, because he is still living within this false reality of nature and believes in it. If a person believes in nature, G-d does not usually change it for him. But a person who realizes that the nature of the world is that it is an arena to do Torah and *mitzvos*, and that it cannot stop him, his nature becomes that: the world will not stop him. Like a *shliach* (emissary) of the Rebbe who realizes that as long as he goes in the Rebbe's powers and just does what the Rebbe tells him, it is normal for everything to work out. That is the reality of the world, so miracles happen all the time. It is *midda k'neged midda* (measure for measure).

phrases.he: וכמו בענין עשרה הרוגי מלוכה
phrases.en: like the ten martyrs

phrases.he: שהעלו מיין נוקבין לאבא ואמא בבחינת הפנימית על ידי מסירת נפש דוקא)
phrases.en: they made a *ha'ala'as MaN* to *pnimiyus* of *Abba*

blocks.text: As explained elsewhere, **like the ten martyrs**, whom we read about on *Yom Kippur*, "soon": through *mesirus nefesh* davka, **they made a ha'ala'as MaN** (a raising of *mayin nukvin*, the receiver's arousal from below) **to pnimiyus of Abba** that was enough to sustain the worlds all the way until *Moshiach* comes. In other words, the pleasure G-d got from what they did fulfilled the purpose of the world enough for it to be worth doing the whole thing until *Moshiach*, just for them. Because what they showed, the idea of *mesirus nefesh*, is not for the Torah and *mitzvos* and not for any purpose: there is an essential connection to G-d, and they showed it. And revealing that is the main thing of the world. They revealed the *yechida* (the essence of the soul), to the inner side of *Abba*.

blocks.title: The interested students
blocks.text: It is like any relationship, a teacher and a student, or a husband and wife. Say you are teaching and working to teach the students: if they put in a lot of effort and show a big interest, that is a *ha'ala'as MaN*. It makes you more motivated, because you feel that they are really interested and want it, so it makes you want to give more. And the same, it works both ways, when a husband feels that his wife is dedicated to him and appreciates him: it motivates him to give more and be more. That is a *ha'ala'as MaN* to the inner side of *Abba*.

When a person has *mesirus nefesh*, selfless dedication, it reveals this essential connection that is higher than anything: that he gives himself over to you. Like when they said *naaseh* before *nishma*: the commitment of the Jews. Our commitment is like the *MaN* to G-d, and His commitment to us is the drawing down of *MaD* (*mayin duchrin*, the giver's flow). So there is a commitment to the *mitzvos*, and then there is *mesirus nefesh* to G-d, which in a way is higher than the *mitzvos*. For here they had *mesirus nefesh* in deed, with their bodies, and they did not gain anything; it was totally just to show that they are for G-d. If G-d wants me to die, I am willing to die, that's it, and to be tortured to death.

blocks.title: The chassid willing to give his life
blocks.text: There is dedication to a subject matter, and then there is being dedicated to you. It inspires a teacher to give a lot more and be a lot more dedicated to his students when they are willing to listen to whatever he says and give up a lot for that, give up everything for the teacher. Imagine a *chassid* of the Rebbe who is willing to give his life away. That is a big *ha'ala'as MaN*.

blocks.title: The Holocaust and Moshiach's delay
blocks.text: And then the Holocaust was in a way even more, because a lot of the time they did not even have a choice, and it was everybody. Like the story where they sing *Ani Maamin*: that kind of thing is "just crazy *ha'ala'as MaN*". "I don't really understand how it's possible to have that kind of stuff happening with *Moshiach* not coming, cuz it's so disproportionate. It's like this huge *ha'ala'as MaN* that's like ridiculous, and then what comes from it?"
